stem: Ilan, a collegiate golfer who transferred this year from a program that played much easier courses, rushes his short putts under pressure. He and his consultant agree to build a pre-putt routine, and Ilan is eager to start it at tomorrow's practice. The consultant wants to be able to show Ilan and his coach later in the season whether the routine itself changed his short putting. Before the routine is introduced, what should the consultant do?
options: Start the routine tomorrow, and log his short-putt makes at every practice from then on
Give him the CSAI-2 before his next event, then repeat it once the season has ended
Chart his short-putt makes and pre-stroke timing over several practices until stable
Pull his putting statistics from last season to serve as the comparison for this season
rationales: Tracking makes from the first day of the routine produces intervention-phase data with nothing to compare them against; without a baseline, later improvement cannot be separated from ordinary practice or familiarity with new courses.
The CSAI-2 measures state anxiety and confidence, not the target behavior of rushed putting, and two administrations months apart are too sparse to link any change to the routine.

In an A–B single-case design, the target behavior is measured repeatedly in a baseline phase until it is stable, and change after the intervention is judged against that baseline. Choosing behavior-specific measures (makes and pre-stroke timing) and collecting them before intervening is part of planning the evaluation.
Last season's statistics come from easier courses, a different program, and different training conditions, so a comparison with them cannot isolate the effect of the routine.
takeaway: Choose a target measure and collect a stable baseline before introducing an intervention, so later change can be judged against it.

stem: A consultant is planning a six-week in-game communication program for a professional esports team. The coach says league win rate is the measure that matters and that he puts little stock in how players say they feel. The schedule pits the team against the league's strongest opponents during those weeks, and a new player joined last month. How should the consultant propose measuring progress?
options: Keep win rate, and add coded counts of clear, timely callouts from recorded matches
Track win rate, and weight each result by the opponent's current league ranking
Replace win rate with weekly player ratings of how well the team communicated
Settle on measures with the coach after the first two weeks show how players respond
rationales: A process measure that directly reflects the targeted skill (the quality of in-game callouts), coded from recordings, is sensitive to the program and objective enough for a skeptical coach. Keeping win rate respects his priority while making the evaluation, and any attribution, realistic.
Weighting by opponent strength makes the outcome fairer, but win rate still depends on the new player, strategy, and much else, so it cannot show whether communication itself improved.
Player ratings are a process measure, but they are the kind of self-report the coach discounts, and dropping his priority measure undermines his buy-in to the evaluation.
Measures should be chosen during planning, before the program starts, so a baseline can be collected and the choice of measures is not shaped by early results.
takeaway: Pair outcome measures with an objective process measure of the targeted skill, and choose them before the program begins.

stem: A consultant will deliver arousal-regulation training to an infantry company before a field training cycle. The commander says, "I don't need to know if they liked it. I need to know whether soldiers actually use this stuff when they're under pressure out there." While planning the evaluation, which measure best answers the commander's question?
options: Soldiers' end-of-training ratings of how likely they are to use breathing and refocusing
A scenario test at the end of training in which soldiers explain when to use each technique
Changes in the company's scores on its next timed live-fire qualification
Squad leaders' structured checklists of breathing and refocusing in later field exercises
rationales: Ratings of intended use, collected before soldiers have faced field pressure, are reaction-level data in Kirkpatrick's terms; intentions often do not match what people do under stress.
A scenario test measures the learning level: it shows soldiers know when a technique applies, not that they use it under pressure in the field.
Qualification scores are a results-level outcome shaped by marksmanship training, equipment, and conditions; they cannot show whether the techniques were actually used.

Whether trainees apply skills in the real performance environment is Kirkpatrick's behavior level. Structured observation by squad leaders during later field exercises, planned before training begins, answers the commander's question directly.
takeaway: Match the evaluation level to the stakeholder's question: using skills in the real setting is Kirkpatrick's behavior level.

stem: A consultant ran four workshops on managing performance anxiety for a professional ballet company. Dancers rated the workshops highly, and a follow-up quiz showed they understood the techniques. Yet during two weeks of rehearsal observation, the consultant saw almost no dancers using them, and several said there is "no time" in the rehearsal schedule, which the artistic staff set. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Run a follow-up workshop that drills each technique in short, rehearsal-length bursts
Work with the artistic staff to build brief practice into rehearsals, then observe again
Give dancers a daily home-practice log, and review the logs with them each week
Report the strong reaction and learning results to the director and continue the program
rationales: Shorter drills may make the techniques feel quicker, but learning has already been shown, and another workshop leaves the scheduling barrier the dancers named untouched.

The evaluation located the breakdown at Kirkpatrick's behavior level, and the dancers named a barrier in the work environment. Transfer depends on a climate that makes room for skill use, so revising the plan with the stakeholders who control rehearsal time and then measuring again is the evidence-based response.
Home practice can build familiarity, but the goal is use during rehearsal and performance, and a home log neither removes the scheduling barrier nor measures transfer to the studio.
Reaction and learning results do not show behavior change; Kirkpatrick's levels are not interchangeable, and continuing unchanged ignores the observation data showing transfer has not happened.
takeaway: When reaction and learning are strong but behavior is not, look for transfer barriers in the environment and revise with the stakeholders who control them.

stem: A consultant tracks an adolescent swimmer's 100-m freestyle times in weekly time trials. Over six baseline weeks, as her training block progressed, her times dropped steadily by about the same amount each week. Imagery training then began, and over the next six weeks her times kept dropping at the same steady rate. What is the most defensible conclusion about imagery from these data?
options: Imagery added to her gains, since her times kept improving throughout the imagery phase
Imagery has been shown not to help her, since training explains all of her improvement
The data cannot be interpreted, since her baseline times were not stable before imagery
No imagery effect is evident, since her rate of improvement held steady at the switch
rationales: Faster times during the imagery phase are exactly what the baseline trend predicted on its own; crediting imagery ignores that trend and is post hoc reasoning.
An A–B comparison on one measure cannot prove the absence of an effect; imagery may still affect other targets such as race-day focus or confidence that these times do not capture.
Baseline stability means predictability, not flatness; a steady, consistent trend is a predictable baseline, so the data are interpretable and simply show no change at the phase shift.

In single-case evaluation, an intervention effect is inferred from a change in level, trend, or variability when the phase changes. Because the improvement seen in baseline (likely from training) continued unchanged, it cannot be attributed to imagery; this is realistic attribution.
takeaway: A single-case effect requires a change in level or trend at the phase change; a continuing baseline trend can't be credited to the intervention.

stem: Midway through a plan to help Folasade, a collegiate softball pitcher, regain composure after issuing a walk, she tells her consultant she feels "way calmer" on the mound. Her pitching coach, however, reports no visible change, and her walk and strikeout numbers are unchanged. Folasade agreed at the outset that the coach could share observations with the consultant. What should the consultant do next?
options: Explore the mismatch with Folasade and add structured observation of her between-pitch routine
Agree with Folasade to keep the plan as it is, since felt calm often comes before visible change
Revise the plan now to target observable behaviors, since the coach and the statistics agree
Have her complete the CSAI-2 before her next start to check the calm she has been reporting
rationales: Triangulating client, coach, and performance data means treating disagreement as information. Exploring the mismatch with the athlete and adding a direct, targeted measure (such as observing her routine after a walk) clarifies whether change is internal only, not yet visible, or absent before the plan is revised.

Internal change can precede visible change, but keeping the plan unchanged without examining the discrepancy leaves the evaluation unresolved and sets aside two sources of data that disagree with her report.
Statistics and a coach's general impression can lag behind or miss process changes; revising midway, before the discrepancy has been explored, is premature.
A second self-report measure adds more of the same kind of data; it cannot resolve a disagreement between how she feels and what others observe.
takeaway: When client, coach, and performance data disagree, explore the discrepancy and add targeted measures before judging the plan.

stem: After a season with a professional rugby club, a consultant wants candid feedback on her own effectiveness from the 30 players she worked with, beyond what the head coach has already told her. Several players have said they would hesitate to criticize her to her face, or anywhere teammates or staff might hear. Which method best fits her goal?
options: Hold brief one-on-one exit interviews in which she asks each player for honest feedback
Ask the club's welfare officer to gather players' views in small group discussions
Distribute a structured consultant evaluation form that players return anonymously
Compare players' pre- and post-season scores on a mental skills questionnaire
rationales: One-on-one interviews keep teammates out of the room, but players have said they hesitate to criticize her directly, so face-to-face feedback is likely to be softened.
Small group discussions put players in front of teammates, which is the setting they are wary of, and routing views through a staff member adds a filter.

Structured consultant evaluation forms, such as the one developed by Partington and Orlick, ask athletes to rate specific consultant characteristics and the usefulness of the service. Anonymous completion reduces social-desirability pressure and fear of exposure, so the feedback is more candid.
Change in players' mental skills is useful outcome evidence, but it does not tell her how players experienced her as a consultant or which of her behaviors to keep or change.
takeaway: Use structured, anonymous consultant evaluation forms to get candid client feedback on your effectiveness.

stem: After a goal-setting session with a high school track team went poorly, a consultant writes a journal entry. It describes what happened (athletes on their phones, little discussion) and how he felt (frustrated, a bit embarrassed), then ends: "Next time I'll be more engaging." His mentor says the plan is too vague to act on. Using Gibbs's reflective cycle, what gap in the entry best explains why his plan is so vague?
options: He has not described the session in enough detail, such as when each athlete disengaged
He has not judged what went well or poorly, or worked out why the session went that way
He has not explored his frustration and embarrassment in enough depth before moving on
He has not named specific activities and timings to use in the next session he leads
rationales: He has already described the session; more detail at the description stage records the problem without producing the sense-making that a specific plan depends on.

Gibbs's cycle moves from description and feelings to evaluation (what was good and bad about the experience) and analysis (making sense of it, for example with theory or context), then to a conclusion and an action plan. Because he skipped evaluation and analysis, he has no basis for a conclusion or for a plan more specific than "be more engaging."
His feelings are already named; dwelling on them further does not supply the evaluation and analysis stages that give the plan its content.
Listing activities treats the symptom: without evaluating and analyzing why the session failed, any specific activities he names are guesses rather than responses to the actual problem.
takeaway: Reflection that jumps from feelings to "do better next time" skips evaluation and analysis, the stages that make a conclusion and action plan specific.

stem: Rosalind, a masters triathlete, has met her goals for managing race-morning worry after four months of work, and she and her consultant agree to end after two more sessions. Her next goal race is overseas, with an unfamiliar course, long travel, and a large time-zone change, and she notes that her current routine assumes her home course and usual sleep. Which focus for the final sessions best supports her keeping her gains after consultation ends?
options: Teach two new worry-management strategies suited to unfamiliar race settings
Book a video check-in for race week in case her worry returns while she travels
Review which skills helped most and compile them into a written race-morning plan
Map the trouble spots that race could pose and rehearse handling each one herself
rationales: New skills introduced in the last two sessions compete with consolidating the ones that already work and risk sending her off with partly learned tools.
A race-week check-in extends support rather than building independence; an optional open door is reasonable, but it does not prepare her to cope with the new demands on her own.
Consolidating what worked is useful, but a plan built around her home routine does not anticipate the unfamiliar course, travel, and sleep disruption she has said her routine does not cover.

Planned termination includes generalization and relapse-prevention planning: anticipating high-risk situations, rehearsing self-directed coping for them, and building the client's independence so skills transfer to new settings after consultation ends.
takeaway: Before ending, build independence: anticipate high-risk situations and rehearse self-directed coping so gains generalize.

stem: A consultant spent a season with a collegiate volleyball team that went on to win its conference title. The athletic director plans a press release this week saying the mental training program "won us the championship" and asks the consultant for a supporting quote. During the same season, the team added a transfer setter and overhauled its strength program. How should the consultant respond?
options: Offer wording that names the program as one contributor, citing its process and behavior data
Approve the quote, and ask that the release also mention the setter and the new strength program
Ask the director to hold the announcement until a formal program evaluation has been completed
Suggest the release credit the athletes' effort and the new staff rather than the program
rationales: A championship is a results-level outcome (Kirkpatrick) with many causes, here including a new setter and a new strength program. Honest evaluation frames the program as a contributor and points to evidence more directly tied to it, such as process and behavior data, which protects the consultant's integrity and credibility.
Listing other factors alongside the quote still endorses the claim that the program won the title, which overstates the evidence and sets the program up to look like a failure in a losing season.
The release is going out this week, and delaying it is not the consultant's call; the season's data already allow an accurate statement of the program's contribution now.
Steering credit entirely to others ignores the program's real evidence; the goal is accurate attribution, not modesty.
takeaway: Present outcomes as multi-causal: claim a contribution, not sole credit, and point to the evidence closest to what the program targeted.

stem: A consultant has worked with Stellan, a conservatory violist preparing for orchestra auditions, on a pre-performance routine. Session logs show he now completes the routine before nearly every mock audition, and his self-rated tension has dropped. His viola teacher has remarked that the routine looks "fussy" onstage, and Stellan is unsure he will keep it once real auditions begin. Which evaluation step best addresses what the consultant needs to learn now?
options: Continue logging routine use through his first real audition to confirm the trend holds
Video his mock auditions and time how much the routine adds before each piece
Ask Stellan and his teacher, in structured interviews, how acceptable and useful it is
Add a validated performance-anxiety inventory to his self-rated tension scores
rationales: More completion data strengthens the evidence that behavior changed, but it cannot capture whether Stellan and his teacher regard the change as worth keeping.
Timing the routine gives an objective view of its length, but whether it looks fussy or fits a performer's life is a judgment only the stakeholders can make.

Social validation asks clients and significant others whether the goals were important, the procedures acceptable, and the effects meaningful in everyday performance life. The teacher's remark and Stellan's doubts are exactly these questions, and interviews complement the behavioral and self-report data already collected.
A second anxiety measure adds detail about tension, which has already improved; it does not address whether the routine is acceptable to the people who will decide whether it continues.
takeaway: Social validation asks clients and stakeholders whether goals, procedures, and outcomes were important, acceptable, and meaningful.

stem: Midway through an Olympic cycle, a consultant to a national rowing team reviews anonymous evaluation forms. Athletes rate her as knowledgeable, trustworthy, and easy to talk to, but many add that her sessions are "interesting but hard to use on the water," and several say the ideas feel "the same for everyone." Based on research on consultant effectiveness with elite athletes, which change should she prioritize?
options: Add case examples from published research on elite rowers to each session
Turn session content into individual strategies rowers practice on the water
Move sessions to the boathouse right before water training so ideas stay fresh
Shorten sessions and send each rower a written summary of the main points
rationales: Research examples may make the content feel more relevant, but they keep it at the level of ideas and leave it identical for every athlete, which is what the feedback criticizes.

Studies of consultant effectiveness with Olympic athletes (Partington and Orlick's evaluation work; Gould and colleagues) found that effective consultants offer clear, practical strategies individualized to the athlete and usable in the sport. The feedback points to exactly that gap.
Holding sessions closer to training changes timing and setting, but the content would still be general and untried in the boat, so the transfer problem remains.
Shorter sessions and summaries change the format of delivery, not its practicality; the same general content would still be hard to apply on the water.
takeaway: Elite athletes value consultants who fit in and give practical, individualized strategies they can use in their sport.

stem: A consultant tried a new trust-building activity with a youth hockey team, and it fell flat: players joked through it and the coach cut it short. That evening he reviewed his notes and observed that the activity ran long, came right after a hard skate, and asked 12-year-olds to share personal stories in front of the group. According to Kolb's experiential learning cycle, what should he do next?
options: Run a shorter version of the activity next week and see whether the response changes
Ask the coach and two players how the activity felt from their side of the room
Write a fuller reflective account of what each player said and did during it
Link what he noticed to theory on group development and early-adolescent disclosure
rationales: Trying a revised version is active experimentation, the final phase of the cycle; doing it before making sense of the observations means the revision is based on a guess rather than an understanding of why the activity failed.
Gathering others' perspectives adds to reflective observation, a phase he has already completed with clear observations; it does not move him forward in the cycle.
A fuller account is more reflective observation; he already has specific observations, and the cycle now calls for interpreting them.

Kolb's cycle runs from concrete experience to reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. Having reflected on what happened, his next step is abstract conceptualization: making sense of the observations with concepts such as age-appropriate disclosure, timing, and group development, which then informs what he tests.
takeaway: In Kolb's cycle, reflection is followed by abstract conceptualization, making sense of the experience with theory, before testing a revised approach.

topic: Ending when the fit is poor
stem: A consultant has met by video with Annika, an elite figure skater, for eight sessions on competition focus. They reviewed progress together at session four and revised the plan, but Annika's ratings and her coach's reports still show little change, and Annika says the cognitive approach "just doesn't click" for her. The consultant's training is mainly in cognitive-behavioral methods. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Raise ending with Annika and name practitioners whose methods could suit her better
Revise the plan a second time, swapping in different cognitive-behavioral techniques
Take a short course in an acceptance-based approach and begin using it with her
Ask her coach whether the consultation should continue, given the lack of change
rationales: When a client is not benefiting despite a joint review and revision, and the mismatch involves the consultant's approach, ethical practice is to discuss ending openly and help the client find a better-fitting provider. This protects her welfare and respects her autonomy.
A second revision within the same framework does not answer her feedback that the cognitive approach itself does not suit her, and it adds time and cost after one revision has already failed.
A brief course does not create competence in a new approach; practicing it with a current client would exceed the consultant's competence, which the Ethics Code asks practitioners to stay within.
The coach is a useful source of observations, but the decision about continuing belongs to Annika and the consultant, and handing it to the coach bypasses her autonomy.
takeaway: When a client isn't benefiting after the plan has been revised, discuss ending and help them find a better-fitting practitioner.

stem: A consultant who works with six executives at a financial firm on performing under pressure accepts a position abroad and will stop consulting altogether in three months. Two of the executives are midway through their plans and want to keep working on their goals with someone. How should the consultant handle these two clients?
options: Line up a trusted colleague to take over, and send her notes ahead so there is no gap
Tell them soon, review their progress, and with their consent arrange a handoff
Keep sessions on track, then discuss referral options with them in the final session
Let the firm's HR lead know which clients need coverage so the firm can arrange it
rationales: Arranging a successor and sending records without the clients' consent breaches confidentiality and takes away their choice about whether, and with whom, to continue.

Ending because of the consultant's own circumstances still calls for planned termination: timely notice, a review of progress, and, with each client's consent, a transition to another qualified provider, sharing information only as the client authorizes.
Waiting until the final session leaves no time to consolidate gains or arrange continuity, which amounts to an abrupt termination even if options are discussed.

Telling the employer which employees are clients and what they need breaches confidentiality unless the clients agreed to it; the firm is a stakeholder but is not entitled to that information by default.
takeaway: When you must end, give timely notice, review progress, and arrange a consented handoff to another provider.

stem: A consultant is introducing a free-throw routine to three wheelchair basketball players in a national-team development squad, and all three will eventually receive it. She wants evidence that the routine, rather than ordinary practice or shared team events, drives any improvement, and she records each player's free-throw percentage at every practice. Which way of introducing the routine would best support that inference?
options: Start the routine for the three together after a two-week baseline, then compare levels
Teach it to two players and keep the third without it as a comparison for the season
Start it with each player at a different point while the others stay in baseline
Start the routine for the three together and add weekly confidence ratings as an outcome
rationales: A shared start after a baseline is an A–B comparison repeated three times; any team-wide influence that coincides with the start, such as a change in practice or the season calendar, cannot be ruled out.
Withholding the routine from one player all season conflicts with the plan for all three to receive it, and a single comparison player who differs in skill and role gives weak evidence.

A multiple-baseline design across participants staggers when the intervention starts. If each player's percentage changes only after the routine is introduced for that player, while players still in baseline stay the same, ordinary practice and shared events become unlikely explanations.
A second outcome adds information about confidence, but with everyone starting at once it still cannot separate the routine's effect from practice or shared events.
takeaway: Staggering the start across individuals (a multiple-baseline design) strengthens causal inference in single-case evaluation.

stem: During a live video workshop on stress management for a fire department's new recruits, a consultant notices that cameras are switching off and the chat has gone quiet ten minutes into her slides. Without stopping the session to plan, she asks recruits to type the situations they expect to find most stressful and builds the rest of the workshop around their answers. Which concept best describes what she did?
options: Reflection-on-action, in which practice is reviewed to improve how it is delivered
Gibbs's evaluation stage, in which the good and bad aspects of an experience are judged
Kolb's active experimentation, in which a new approach is tried out in practice
Reflection-in-action, in which a practitioner reshapes practice as it unfolds
rationales: Reflection-on-action is Schön's term for looking back on practice after it is over to learn from it; she changed course during the session itself.
Gibbs's evaluation stage is part of a structured cycle completed after an experience, judging what went well and poorly; she acted in the moment rather than working through a reflective cycle.
Active experimentation in Kolb's cycle tests ideas formed through reflection and conceptualization on an earlier experience; her change came from noticing and responding within the same experience.

Schön distinguished reflection-in-action, thinking and adjusting while practice is unfolding, from reflection-on-action, reviewing afterward. Noticing disengagement and reshaping the workshop on the spot is reflection-in-action.
takeaway: Reflection-in-action is adjusting during the session; reflection-on-action is the structured review afterward. Skilled consultants use both.

stem: A consultant's season-long contract with a collegiate lacrosse team ends after the final tournament. Over the year she ran team sessions, met with individual athletes, and began training the coaching staff to lead short pre-practice focus routines. The head coach wants those routines to continue next season without her. Which plan best concludes the consultation?
options: Hold a closing team session, coach the staff as they lead routines, and set a follow-up plan
Write a detailed manual of the routines and leave it with the coaching staff for next season
Give the head coach a written summary of each athlete's progress to carry into next season
Run a final session on two advanced skills, and leave practice guides with the staff
rationales: Ending with a team is a planned process: a closing session to review and consolidate, building the staff's capacity through guided practice so the work is sustainable once the consultant leaves, and an agreed follow-up or open-door arrangement within the contract's terms.
A manual records the routines, but staff whose training is unfinished need guided practice leading them, and a document alone provides no closure with the team or follow-up.
Individual athletes' progress and what they discussed are confidential; a summary for the coach requires each athlete's consent and must match what was agreed at the outset.
New skills at the very end dilute consolidation and leave the staff trying to sustain skills the team never established, even with written guides.
takeaway: Conclude team work with a closing session, a handoff of routines to staff, and agreed follow-up, while keeping individual content confidential.

stem: A newly certified consultant in solo private practice reviews end-of-program evaluation forms from three different teams. On all three, athletes rate her strategies as useful but repeatedly comment that she "talks more than she listens" in individual sessions. She has new contracts starting next month. What is the most appropriate next step for her professional development?
options: Record sessions with client consent and review them on her own for talk-to-listen ratio
Arrange peer consultation or mentoring to review her sessions and set a listening goal
Ask each client at the end of each session to rate how well she listened that day
Enroll in a graduate counseling-skills course before her next contracts begin
rationales: Self-review of recordings is a useful tool, but reviewing alone is prone to the same blind spots the feedback revealed, and it does not add the outside perspective and accountability of consultation.

A theme that recurs across independent evaluations is credible feedback. Taking it to peer consultation or a mentor (for example, reviewing session recordings or detailed case notes with client consent) and setting a concrete skill goal is how practitioners turn evaluation data into reflective, ongoing development.
Session-by-session ratings collected face to face invite socially desirable answers, and gathering more data does not by itself build the skill the existing feedback already identified.
A formal course may build general skills, but it cannot be completed before her contracts begin, and it does not give targeted feedback on her own sessions.
takeaway: Treat consistent client feedback as data for growth: take it to peer consultation or mentoring and set a specific skill goal.

stem: Darnell, a 45-year-old office manager, is working with a consultant on building a consistent running habit before a charity 10K. His training logs show he met his weekly target for six straight weeks, then dropped to about half of it in weeks seven and eight. Nothing in the plan has changed. What should the consultant do first?
options: Lower his weekly target for now, then raise it again once he is back on track
Add a small reward for each week he meets his target, starting this week
Go over the last two weeks' logs with Darnell to learn what changed
Readminister his exercise motivation questionnaire to check for a drop in motivation
rationales: Lowering the target may help eventually, but adjusting the plan before understanding the cause may not address the real barrier and could discard a target that worked for six weeks.
A reward adds a new technique before anyone knows why the drop happened; if the barrier is a schedule change or an injury, the reward will not help.

Monitoring data signal that something changed but not why. Reassessing collaboratively with the client (for example, a new work schedule, a minor injury, or fading motivation) identifies the barrier so that any revision is targeted and the client stays engaged in the plan.
A questionnaire assumes the cause is motivational; talking through the logs with him can surface practical barriers, such as work or injury, that a motivation scale would miss.
takeaway: When monitoring data shift, reassess with the client to learn why before revising the plan.
